## The question

Large language models (LLMs) now write working code in seconds. So why should an economist still learn to write it?

Econometric work typically moves through five steps:

> **question → identification → estimation → implementation → empirical application**

This course focuses on the last two steps — and on the **replication packages** that make them verifiable.

## Where we are going

Two capabilities are the destination of the course.

**Reproduce.**
: Document and archive the computational environment, data, and code in public archives, so that anyone can obtain your results again.

**Audit.**
: Assess the reproducibility of other researchers' replication packages, and so help sustain the integrity of empirical research.

## How we get there

We build toward those two capabilities through four practices that you carry out yourself.

| Practice | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Formulate** | Translate research and business questions into well-posed computational problems. |
| **Simulate** | Build worlds in which the truth is known — including *both* potential outcomes for every unit — and check whether an estimator recovers the causal effect. |
| **Evaluate** | Judge whether code written by an LLM computes the quantity you intend. |
| **Debug** | Diagnose and fix errors — both the ones that stop your program and the silent ones that do not. |

### Why *Evaluate* needs an economist

Code that follows generic programming conventions can run without error and still compute the wrong estimand, mis-implement the identification strategy, or mishandle data.

A common example is silently dropping every observation that has a missing value (*listwise deletion*). General-purpose data-cleaning advice often recommends it. But in household earnings data, nonresponse is not random: it is highest in *both tails* of the earnings distribution [@bollinger2019]. Dropping those observations therefore distorts exactly the inequality measures an economist cares about.

### You cannot evaluate what you have never written

In a randomized experiment with 52 junior engineers learning a new Python library, participants who used an AI assistant scored 50% on a follow-up comprehension quiz, versus 67% for those who coded by hand. The gap was largest on debugging questions. Participants who asked the assistant only *conceptual* questions kept most of the learning [@shen2026].

This course is designed around that finding. You will use LLMs — but in ways that keep the understanding with you.
